lesson:
# Device models and corners in a PDK

A PDK's device models describe how each transistor behaves across voltage, temperature and process variation. Corners bound the global spread, statistical models describe mismatch, and layout-dependent parameters carry context. Every timing library, every circuit simulation and every power estimate is computed from these models, so their structure decides what margin a design must carry.

## Corners for global variation

Transistors vary from lot to lot and wafer to wafer. Foundries summarize this with process corners named by NMOS then PMOS speed: TT (typical), SS (slow-slow), FF (fast-fast), and the skewed SF and FS. Skewed corners matter for circuits that depend on the ratio of NMOS to PMOS strength, such as SRAM cells, level shifters and ratioed logic. Each corner is combined with supply voltage and temperature to define a PVT corner, and Liberty libraries are characterized at each. Slow corners at low voltage bound setup timing; fast corners at high voltage and temperature bound leakage and hold.

## Statistical models and mismatch

Corners stack worst cases and can be pessimistic, or miss combinations. Statistical models describe parameter distributions so Monte Carlo simulation can sample real behaviour. They separate global variation, shared by all devices on a die, from local mismatch between nominally identical neighbours, which comes from random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness and work-function granularity. Pelgrom's law says mismatch standard deviation scales as $1/\sqrt{WL}$: quadrupling gate area halves mismatch sigma. Library characterization uses these models to produce variation-aware timing data, such as Liberty variation format tables. Those tables let a timer carry sigma per arc instead of a flat margin.

## Layout dependence, aging and model maturity

A transistor's threshold and mobility depend on its surroundings: distance to the well edge (well proximity effect), length of diffusion and distance to diffusion breaks (stress effects), and neighbouring gate density. Extraction measures these distances and passes them as instance parameters so simulation sees the layout context. Reliability models add end-of-life shifts from bias temperature instability and hot-carrier injection, which feed aging-aware timing margins. Device corners and interconnect RC corners are separate because FEOL and BEOL vary from different steps. Early models are projections and are re-fitted as silicon data arrives, so timing results carry the model version.

## Going deeper

Pelgrom, Duinmaijer and Welbers, "Matching properties of MOS transistors", IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits (1989); the BSIM-CMG technical manual from the BSIM group at UC Berkeley.

lesson:
# Dies per wafer and edge loss

How many dies a wafer holds is the denominator of every cost-per-die calculation and an input to yield and DTCO trade-offs. Rectangular dies do not tile a circle, so the count is less than wafer area over die area, and the loss is worst for large dies. A standard closed-form estimate captures the edge loss well enough for early studies, and exact counts come from placing the die grid.

## Area ratio as an upper bound

The crude estimate divides wafer area by die area. A 300 mm wafer has area $\pi \times 150^2 = 70{,}686$ mm^2. A 10 mm by 10 mm die gives a ratio of 706.9. That number is an upper bound: it counts fractional dies at the edge and ignores the area that partial dies waste. It is still useful as a sanity check, and the gap between it and the real count grows with die size because the wasted ring around the edge is roughly one die deep. Larger dies waste a deeper ring.

## The edge-loss formula

A widely used estimate subtracts a term for the edge: $DPW = \pi d^2/(4A) - \pi d/\sqrt{2A}$, with wafer diameter $d$ and die area $A$. The second term approximates the number of dies lost along the circumference: the circumference $\pi d$ divided by the die diagonal $\sqrt{2A}$. For $d = 300$ mm and $A = 100$ mm^2: $706.9 - 942.5/14.14 = 706.9 - 66.6 = 640.2$, so about 640 dies. For a 400 mm^2 die the area term is 176.7 and the edge term 33.3, leaving 143: edge loss is 19% for the large die against 9% for the small one.

## Edge exclusion, scribe lanes and exact counts

Two corrections matter in practice. The edge exclusion removes a ring of width $e$, so the usable diameter is $d - 2e$. Scribe lanes, the saw streets between dies that also carry test structures, enlarge the die pitch to $(w + s)(h + s)$. A 10 by 10 mm die with 0.1 mm scribe on a 300 mm wafer with 3 mm exclusion uses $d = 294$ and $A = 102.01$, giving $665.6 - 64.7 = 600$ dies. Exact counts come from placing the die grid and counting dies entirely inside the usable circle; tools also optimize the grid offset, which can gain several dies. Die aspect ratio matters too, which floorplanners can exploit.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Defect density and yield models

Random particles and process defects land on wafers with some average density. A die that receives a killer defect fails. Turning a defect density into a yield needs a statistical model, and the simplest, the Poisson model, already shows why yield falls exponentially with die area, which is the main economic pressure on die size and on chiplets.

## Expected defects per die

Let $D_0$ be the density of killer defects per unit area, and $A$ the die area. The expected number of killer defects per die is $\lambda = A D_0$. Units must match: die area is usually given in mm^2 and defect density in defects per cm^2, and 100 mm^2 is 1 cm^2. A 150 mm^2 die at 0.2 defects per cm^2 has $\lambda = 1.5 \times 0.2 = 0.3$. A mature process may run at around 0.1 per cm^2 or lower; an early process runs higher, and that early defect density is a major reason large dies are expensive on new nodes.

## The Poisson yield model

If defects land independently and uniformly, the count on a die is Poisson with mean $\lambda$, and the die works only with zero defects: $Y = e^{-\lambda} = e^{-A D_0}$. For $\lambda = 0.3$, $Y = 74.1\%$. Doubling the die area to $\lambda = 0.6$ gives 54.9%: the yield of the larger die is the square of the smaller one's. That exponential dependence is the core of yield economics. Combined with dies per wafer, it means a die twice the area yields well under half as many good dies per wafer.

## Inverting yield to learn defect density

Foundries and product teams run the model backwards: from measured yield infer an effective defect density, $D_0 = -\ln Y / A$. A 200 mm^2 die yielding 80% implies $D_0 = -\ln 0.8/2 = 0.112$ per cm^2. That inferred density lumps together all mechanisms, so it is only meaningful if systematic losses have been separated out. The Poisson model also tends to be pessimistic for large dies because real defects cluster; clustered models, discussed next, give higher yield at the same mean density. Product teams track the inferred density over time as a learning curve.

## Going deeper

label: Clustered defects and negative binomial yield
lesson:
# Clustered defects and negative binomial yield

Real defects are not spread uniformly: they cluster on some wafers, in some regions and on some dies. Clustering leaves more dies with zero defects than the Poisson model predicts. The negative binomial model captures this with one extra parameter and is the standard industrial yield model for random defects.

## A gamma-mixed Poisson

Suppose each die's defect count is Poisson, but its mean varies from die to die following a gamma distribution with mean $A D_0$ and shape $\alpha$. Averaging the Poisson zero-probability over that gamma gives $Y = (1 + A D_0/\alpha)^{-\alpha}$. Small $\alpha$ means strong clustering; as $\alpha \to \infty$ the gamma collapses to its mean and the model returns to Poisson, since $(1 + x/\alpha)^{-\alpha} \to e^{-x}$. With $A D_0 = 0.6$ and $\alpha = 2$: $Y = (1.3)^{-2} = 59.2\%$. Typical fitted values of $\alpha$ lie between about 0.5 and 5.

## Comparing with Poisson

At the same mean defect count, clustering raises yield because some dies receive several defects while others receive none. For $A D_0 = 0.6$: Poisson gives 54.9%, the negative binomial with $\alpha = 2$ gives 59.2%, a 4.3-point difference; with $\alpha = 0.5$ it gives $(2.2)^{-0.5} = 67.4\%$. The gap grows with die area. A cost model that uses Poisson will overstate the penalty of a large die when defects cluster strongly. Choosing $\alpha$ is a fitting problem: the foundry fits it to wafer maps, often by counting how yield changes with the size of a block of dies.

## Inferring defect density with clustering

Inverting the model gives $D_0 = \alpha(Y^{-1/\alpha} - 1)/A$. For a 200 mm^2 die yielding 80% with $\alpha = 2$: $0.8^{-0.5} = 1.118$, so $D_0 = 2 \times 0.118/2 = 0.118$ per cm^2, slightly higher than the Poisson estimate of 0.112. The two models agree when yield is high and disagree as yield falls. Murphy's and Seeds' models are older alternatives built from other assumed distributions of defect density. For design decisions, what matters is consistency: compare options with the same model and parameters, and note that chiplet trade-offs are sensitive to the model chosen.

label: Critical area analysis
lesson:
# Critical area analysis

Not every defect that lands on a die kills it. A small extra particle between widely spaced wires is harmless; the same particle between two minimum-spaced wires is a short. Critical area is the region of the layout where the centre of a defect of a given size must fall to cause a failure. It turns a layout into a yield number and tells a DFM tool where spreading or widening wires pays off.

## Shorts between two parallel wires

Model a defect as a conducting disc of diameter $x$. Two parallel wires a distance $s$ apart, running together for length $L$, are shorted if the disc touches both. Along the direction across the gap, the disc centre must lie in a band of width $x - s$, and nothing happens if $x \le s$. Ignoring end effects, the critical area for shorts is $A_c(x) = L \max(0, x - s)$. For $L = 500$ um, $s = 30$ nm and $x = 70$ nm: $A_c = 500$ um $\times 0.040$ um $= 20$ um^2. A defect of 25 nm has zero critical area here, however many land.

## Opens in a single wire

A missing-material defect opens a wire of width $w$ only if it spans the whole width. Its centre must lie in a band of width $x - w$ along the wire, so $A_c^{open}(x) = L \max(0, x - w)$. For $w = 24$ nm, $L = 500$ um and $x = 70$ nm, that is 23 um^2. The two mechanisms pull in opposite directions: widening a wire reduces open critical area but, at fixed pitch, narrows the space and increases short critical area. A DFM optimizer balances them using the relative densities of extra-material and missing-material defects on each layer.

## Critical area of a layout

For a bus of $n$ parallel wires there are $n - 1$ gaps and $n$ wires, so the total critical area at size $x$ is $(n-1) L \max(0, x - s) + n L \max(0, x - w)$, ignoring defects that span three wires. For a real layout, tools compute critical area by geometry: grow every shape by $x/2$ and intersect the grown shapes of different nets; the overlap area is where a defect centre causes a short. Repeating for many defect sizes, with plane sweeps or spatial indices for speed, gives $A_c(x)$, which is then weighted by the defect size distribution to get the expected fault count.

lesson:
# Average critical area over defect sizes

Critical area depends on defect size, and defects come in a distribution of sizes. Averaging critical area over that distribution gives one number per layer and mechanism, the average critical area, which multiplies the total defect density to give the expected fault count. For the common $1/x^3$ size distribution, a wire pair has a clean closed form that makes the dependence on spacing explicit.

## The defect size distribution

Measured defect size distributions fall off steeply for sizes above the smallest that inspection or physics produces. A standard model is $f(x) = 2x_0^2/x^3$ for $x \ge x_0$, normalized because $\int_{x_0}^\infty 2x_0^2 x^{-3}\, dx = 1$. The fraction of defects larger than $x$ is $P(X > x) = (x_0/x)^2$. With $x_0 = 20$ nm, 25% of defects exceed 40 nm and only 4% exceed 100 nm. Small defects are common but usually harmless; large ones are rare but can short wires that are far apart. The weighting of the two is what the average captures.

## Averaging the short critical area

For two wires with spacing $s \ge x_0$ and parallel length $L$, the average short critical area is $\bar A = \int_s^\infty L(x - s) \frac{2x_0^2}{x^3} dx$. The antiderivative of $(x - s)/x^3$ is $-1/x + s/(2x^2)$, which runs from $-1/(2s)$ at $x = s$ to 0 at infinity, so the integral is $1/(2s)$ and $\bar A = L x_0^2/s$. For $L = 1000$ um, $x_0 = 20$ nm and $s = 40$ nm: $\bar A = 1000 \times 400/40$ nm um $= 10{,}000$ nm um $= 10$ um^2. Average critical area is inversely proportional to spacing: doubling the space halves it.

## From average critical area to yield

The expected number of faults on a layer is $\lambda = D_0 \bar A$, where $D_0$ is the total density of the defect type, and with Poisson statistics $Y = e^{-\lambda}$. Suppose a die has 100 m of minimum-spaced wire at 40 nm spacing and $x_0 = 20$ nm. Then $\bar A = 10^8$ um $\times 400/40$ nm $= 10^9$ nm um $= 10^6$ um^2 $= 0.01$ cm^2, and with $D_0 = 0.5$ per cm^2, $\lambda = 0.005$ and $Y = 99.5\%$ for this layer and mechanism. Multiplying such yields over layers and mechanisms gives the random-defect yield. This calculation is why wire spreading targets minimum-spaced runs: they dominate $\bar A$.

## Going deeper

Stapper, "Modeling of integrated circuit defect sensitivities" (1983); Ferris-Prabhu, "Role of defect size distribution in yield modeling", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (1985).

lesson:
# Cost per good die

The economic figure of merit for silicon is the cost of a die that works. It combines wafer cost, dies per wafer and yield in one ratio. Every DTCO, chiplet and die-size decision is ultimately compared through it, and its non-linear dependence on area is why architects care about every square millimetre.

## From wafer cost to die cost

A processed wafer has a cost $C_w$ that covers depreciation, materials, labour and masks amortized over volume; advanced-node wafers cost many thousands of dollars. Before yield, each candidate die costs $C_w/DPW$. A wafer costing 10,000 US dollars with 640 candidate dies gives 15.63 dollars per candidate. Testing, packaging and final test add further costs per die, but the silicon cost is where die area enters most strongly, through both the dies-per-wafer count and the yield. Mask cost, by contrast, is fixed per design and is amortized over volume, so it dominates for low-volume products and vanishes per die for high-volume ones.

## Dividing by good dies

Only good dies can be sold, so cost per good die is $C_{good} = C_w/(DPW \cdot Y)$. With the same wafer, a 100 mm^2 die at 0.2 defects per cm^2 has $Y = e^{-0.2} = 0.819$, so $640 \times 0.819 = 524$ good dies and 19.08 dollars each. A 200 mm^2 die on the same wafer gets about 306 candidates and $Y = e^{-0.4} = 0.670$, so 205 good dies at 48.75 dollars: doubling the area raised cost per good die by a factor of 2.55. Area is penalized twice, once in the count and once in the yield.

## Shrinks and node transitions

A node transition shrinks a design but raises wafer cost. If the die shrinks to 60% of its area while wafer cost rises by 30%, cost per good die changes by $1.3 \times (DPW \cdot Y)_{old}/(DPW \cdot Y)_{new}$. For the 100 mm^2 example, 60 mm^2 gives about 1092 candidates and yield $e^{-0.12} = 0.887$, so 968 good dies at 13.42 dollars, a ratio of 0.70. If defect density on the new node starts higher, the gain shrinks or reverses. This arithmetic, applied to block-level area from DTCO studies, decides whether a technology option is worth its added process cost.

## Going deeper

Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach", chapter 1 on the cost of an integrated circuit; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits", chapter 1.

lesson:
# Design for manufacturability and yield

Design for manufacturability (DFM) changes a legal layout to make it more robust: fewer shapes sensitive to random defects, fewer patterns that print poorly, more redundancy where a single failure would kill the chip. The changes are optional and cost area, capacitance or runtime, so DFM tools score candidates and apply fixes where they are cheap. Their inputs are critical area, recommended rules, hotspot patterns and via counts.

## Layout fixes that buy yield

The standard post-route DFM moves target random defects. Via doubling adds a second via beside each single one where space allows, so a location fails only if both fail. Wire spreading moves wires off minimum spacing into free tracks, lowering short critical area. Wire widening raises the width of long wires to lower open critical area. Recommended rules (longer line-end extensions, larger enclosures, wider spaces near line ends) reduce sensitivity to lithography and overlay variation. Each fix adds capacitance or area, so routers and DFM engines treat them as soft costs to apply where slack and space exist.

## Redundant vias by the numbers

If each via fails open independently with probability $p$ and a design has $N$ single vias, via-limited yield is $(1 - p)^N \approx e^{-Np}$. With $N = 5 \times 10^7$ and $p = 2 \times 10^{-8}$: $Np = 1$ and $Y = 36.8\%$. Doubling every via makes each location fail only with probability $p^2 = 4 \times 10^{-16}$, so $e^{-N p^2} \approx 1 - 2 \times 10^{-8}$, essentially 100%. Linearizing as $1 - Np$ would give zero here, which shows why the exponential form matters. Real redundant vias are not perfectly independent, since a defect large enough can take out both, but the improvement is still large.

## Systematic versus random yield

Random-defect yield follows defect statistics and critical area. Systematic yield loss comes from specific layout patterns that fail under process variation: litho hotspots, CMP-sensitive density regions, stress-sensitive structures. Total yield is often modelled as $Y = Y_{sys} \cdot Y_{rand}$, which assumes the mechanisms are independent. Early in a node's life systematic loss dominates, so flows use litho simulation and pattern matching against libraries of known-bad patterns to find and fix hotspots. As the process matures, random defects become the larger share and critical-area-driven fixes matter more. Separating the two in silicon data takes care, since both appear as failed dies.

## Going deeper

label: Standard-cell architecture and DTCO
lesson:
# Standard-cell architecture and DTCO

A standard-cell library fixes a cell height, a set of routing tracks inside each cell, power rails at the top and bottom, and a gate grid along the width. Those choices couple process pitches to logic density. Design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) treats them as variables, and track height is the first one: how many metal tracks tall a cell is.

## Cell height as tracks times pitch

Cell height is written in tracks of the horizontal routing layer: a 6-track (6T) library on a 28 nm metal pitch is $6 \times 28 = 168$ nm tall. Those tracks hold the cell's internal wiring, the pins the router reaches, and a share of the power rails at the cell boundaries, shared with the abutting rows above and below. Libraries at older nodes used 9 to 12 tracks; FinFET nodes moved to about 7.5 and 6, and recent nodes to around 5. Fractional values such as 7.5 arise when the rails are wider than one track or when the cell grid is not an integer number of pitches.

## Why track height is a DTCO variable

Fewer tracks shrink every cell, but each track removed takes away internal wiring resources and pin access for the router. A cell must still fit its transistors: fewer tracks force fewer fins per device or a different device architecture. Rails must still carry current: narrowing them raises IR drop and electromigration risk, which pushes toward buried or backside power. The cell height reaches the router as the row pitch and as the number of pin access points, so a library that looks smaller can route worse. DTCO evaluates track height by its effect on routed block area and timing, not by cell area alone.

## Area arithmetic of a track reduction

At fixed metal pitch and fixed cell widths, cell area scales with track height. Going from 7.5T to 6T cuts cell area by $1 - 6/7.5 = 20\%$; from 6T to 5T, by 16.7%. Whether a block shrinks as much depends on achievable placement utilization: if fewer tracks raise congestion, the placer must spread cells and the block may shrink only a fraction of the cell gain. A useful habit for a tool designer is to report both numbers, the cell-level reduction and the routed block reduction, and to look for the mechanism when they differ: pin access, power rails or local congestion.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Contacted poly pitch and cell width

The width of a standard cell is counted in contacted poly pitches (CPP): the pitch of the gate lines, including room for a source-drain contact between neighbouring gates. CPP times the number of gate positions, plus whatever the cell boundary needs, sets cell width. Together with metal pitch and track height it gives the basic area scaling metric of a node.

## Cell width in gate pitches

Gates in a modern library sit on a fixed grid. A cell with $g$ gate positions spans about $g$ CPPs, plus space at its boundary to isolate it from its neighbour. With a single diffusion break, which cuts the active region under one dummy gate shared between abutting cells, each cell adds one CPP: width $= (g + 1)\,\mathrm{CPP}$. With a double diffusion break the isolation takes two gate positions: $(g + 2)\,\mathrm{CPP}$. A NAND2 at 48 nm CPP is $3 \times 48 = 144$ nm wide with single diffusion break and 192 nm with double, a 33% difference.

## Row length from a cell list

Because every cell is an integer number of CPPs, row utilization is arithmetic on CPP counts. A row holding an INV (1 gate), a NAND2 (2), an AOI22 (4) and a DFF (about 12) with single diffusion breaks uses $2 + 3 + 5 + 13 = 23$ CPPs, which at 48 nm is 1.104 um. Placement legalizers snap cells to these sites, and filler cells fill the gaps. The diffusion-break style matters for density: single diffusion break saves one CPP per cell boundary, which across a block of small cells is several percent of area, at the cost of a harder isolation process.

## Area scaling between nodes

A common first-order logic density metric multiplies CPP by the cell height, itself track count times metal pitch. Node A at CPP 54 nm, 6 tracks and 36 nm pitch gives $54 \times 6 \times 36$; node B at CPP 48 nm, 6 tracks and 30 nm pitch gives a ratio of $(48 \times 30)/(54 \times 36) = 74.1\%$. Cutting a half track adds another factor of $5.5/6$. Real density gains also depend on diffusion-break style, gate contact placement, and how well blocks route, so foundries quote density on representative mixes of cells. For a tool designer, CPP and metal pitch are the grid every placer and router works on.

label: Fin depopulation
lesson:
# Fin depopulation

In a FinFET library, each transistor's drive comes from a whole number of fins. Fin depopulation reduces the fin count per device, for example from three to two or from two to one, so that the active area, and the cell height, can shrink. It trades drive strength for density and is one of the main levers that let track heights fall.

## Drive scales with fin count

Each fin contributes roughly the same effective channel width, so drive current scales with the number of fins: going from three fins to two keeps about 66.7% of the drive, and from two to one, 50%. Input capacitance falls in the same proportion, so a gate driving another depopulated gate loses less speed than the drive ratio suggests; wire-dominated loads feel the full loss. Width is therefore quantized: designers cannot size a FinFET continuously, only in fin steps, and libraries offer drive variants by fins and fingers. Multi-finger devices recover drive at the cost of cell width.

## Cell height on the fin grid

Fins sit on a fixed fin pitch, and the cell height must contain the NMOS fins, the PMOS fins, the gap between the two regions, and the space at the rails. Written in fin pitches, a cell with $n$ fins per device and $g$ overhead pitches is $(2n + g)$ fin pitches tall. With a 30 nm fin pitch, two fins per device and four overhead pitches give $8 \times 30 = 240$ nm; depopulating to one fin gives $6 \times 30 = 180$ nm. Each fin removed per device takes two fin pitches out of the cell, which must then match a smaller metal track count.

## Drive density and its limits

Depopulation cuts drive faster than area when overhead is fixed. From two fins to one with four overhead pitches, drive halves and height falls from 8 to 6 pitches, so drive per unit area falls to $(1/6)/(2/8) = 0.667$. For logic dominated by small cells and short wires, the density gain outweighs this; for high-performance paths, designers mix taller, higher-drive cells. Depopulation also raises variability, since fewer fins average out less random variation. Gate-all-around nanosheets restore a continuous width knob, since sheet width can vary, which changes how this trade is made at the next nodes.

## Going deeper

Liebmann et al., DTCO papers on fin depopulation and track-height scaling in Proc. SPIE; Hu, "Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits", chapter on FinFETs.

lesson:
# Buried power rails

In a conventional cell, the power and ground rails run along the top and bottom edges on the lowest metal layer and take up track space. A buried power rail (BPR) moves them below the transistors, into the substrate or shallow trench isolation, and connects to the devices from beneath. The freed tracks can shrink the cell or be returned to signal routing, and the rail can be made taller, which lowers its resistance.

## Rails that consume tracks

Front-side rails are wide wires on the M0 or M1 layer at the cell boundary, shared half-and-half with the abutting rows. Together they typically occupy one to two tracks' worth of a cell's height. A 6-track cell with 1.5 tracks of rails has 4.5 tracks for signals. Burying the rails removes them from the routing layer: at a 24 nm pitch, a cell keeping its 4.5 signal tracks drops from $6 \times 24 = 144$ nm to $4.5 \times 24 = 108$ nm, a 25% reduction, if nothing else limits height.

## Lower rail resistance

A buried rail does not compete for routing tracks, so it can be narrow but tall. A front-side M0 rail 30 nm wide and 40 nm thick has cross-section 1200 nm^2; a buried rail 20 nm wide and 120 nm tall has 2400 nm^2, half the resistance per unit length at the same resistivity. Lower rail resistance reduces IR drop along the row, which is an increasing problem as rails narrow. The rail metal must survive the remaining front-end processing, which limits the materials, since copper cannot be used so early in the flow; refractory metals such as tungsten or ruthenium are candidates.

## What buried rails change in the flow

Buried rails connect to source and drain through a via from below, and to the power grid either from the front through vias that pass beside the devices or from the back through nano-through-silicon vias. That second option is a step toward full backside power delivery. For design tools, BPR changes the cell template, the extraction stack, the power-grid model and possibly the placement rules near rail taps. A DTCO study weighs the area and IR gains against new process steps, reliability risks of a metal near the transistors, and the cost of the new masks.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Backside power delivery

Backside power delivery (BSPDN) builds the power distribution network on the back of a thinned wafer and feeds the transistors from below. The front side then carries only signals. It attacks two problems at once: IR drop through tall front-side via stacks and the routing tracks lost to rails and power straps. It also changes the thermal path and the models of several EDA engines.

## Power from the back of the wafer

After the front-side devices and wiring are built, the wafer is bonded face-down to a carrier wafer and the original substrate is ground and etched until the device layer is only a short distance from the new surface. Backside vias, sometimes called nano-through-silicon vias, then connect a backside metal network either to buried power rails or directly to the transistors' source and drain. Thick, low-resistance backside metal layers form the global grid and connect to the package. The front side keeps its signal stack with the power rails and straps removed.

## IR drop with and without backside power

On the front side, current from the package bumps descends the whole metal stack to reach the cells. A path through ten via levels, each with four vias of 5 ohm in parallel, has $10 \times 5/4 = 12.5$ ohm. At 2 mA that is 25 mV of IR drop before the rails. A backside path of 2 ohm drops 4 mV, saving 21 mV. Lower IR drop lets a design run at lower supply margin or higher frequency, and power-grid analysis must be rebuilt for the new stack. The comparison also ignores the rails themselves, which are shorter and wider on the back.

## Trade-offs and tool consequences

Backside power frees front-side tracks and removes power straps, which reduces congestion and can let cells shrink. It costs wafer bonding, thinning and extra metal levels, and it changes the heat path: the bulk silicon that spread heat to the sink is gone, replaced by bonding layers and a carrier, so thermal analysis matters more. Engines that need new models include power-grid and IR analysis, extraction for both sides, placement legalization near backside taps, and thermal simulation. A DTCO comparison of buried-rail front-side delivery against backside delivery must therefore look at routed block PPA, IR drop, temperature and wafer cost together.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# The DTCO evaluation loop

Design-technology co-optimization is an engineering loop, not a single calculation. Candidate process options and cell architectures are turned into rules and models, then into libraries, then into placed and routed benchmark blocks, whose power, performance, area and cost decide which option survives. Every engine in the EDA flow runs inside the loop, which is why tool designers are part of technology definition.

## What DTCO optimizes

The variables are coupled design and technology knobs: CPP, metal pitches, track height, fins or sheets per device, diffusion-break style, rail scheme, contact architecture, and the rules each implies. The objective is block-level power, performance and area at a target, plus wafer cost and yield. Device metrics alone mislead: a faster transistor that needs a taller cell or adds parasitics can lose at the block level. Early in a node's definition there is no signoff PDK, so the loop uses a pathfinding or predictive PDK with projected rules and compact models, and it updates them as process data arrives.

## The loop step by step

For each candidate: write the rules and technology files; generate or draw cell layouts and check them; characterize the cells from the models into timing and power libraries; synthesize, place and route several benchmark blocks; extract and time them; record area, frequency, power and routability. Then compare candidates at matched targets and feed the mechanisms behind wins and losses back into the next candidates. Several benchmarks are needed because a CPU core, a GPU tile and a memory controller stress pin density and wiring differently. A cell that is 12% smaller can give a block only 3% smaller if fewer tracks forced lower utilization.

## From DTCO to STCO

Interpreting results takes care: cell-level metrics such as NAND2 area are proxies that can be optimized at the expense of routability. When a candidate loses frequency on one block, DTCO looks for compensating knobs and reruns rather than accepting or discarding it outright. System-technology co-optimization (STCO) widens the scope to how a system is partitioned across dies, packages and 3D stacks, which technology each part uses, and how memory is attached. The arithmetic of cost per good die, yield versus area, and interface overhead then joins the PPA results, as the next concept on chiplets shows.

## Going deeper

label: System-technology co-optimization and chiplets
lesson:
# System-technology co-optimization and chiplets

System-technology co-optimization asks how to split a system across dies and packages. Splitting a large die into chiplets raises yield, since yield falls exponentially with area, but adds interface area, assembly cost and assembly yield loss. The trade is computed with the same yield and cost arithmetic as a single die, and its answer depends on defect density and die size.

## The monolithic baseline

Start with a monolithic die of area $A$. On a 300 mm wafer costing $C_w$, with dies per wafer from the edge-loss formula and Poisson yield $e^{-A D_0}$, the cost per good die is $C_w/(DPW \cdot Y)$. A 600 mm^2 die has $DPW = 117.8 - 27.2 = 90$ and, at 0.2 defects per cm^2, $Y = e^{-1.2} = 0.301$. At 15,000 dollars per wafer that is $15000/(90 \times 0.301) = 553.4$ dollars per good die. Large dies on a young process are punished by yield, which is the motivation for splitting.

## Splitting into chiplets

Split the design into $k$ chiplets, each $A/k$ plus an overhead fraction for die-to-die interfaces. With $k = 4$ and 10% overhead, each chiplet is 165 mm^2, giving 376 per wafer and $Y = e^{-0.33} = 0.719$, so a good chiplet costs $15000/(376 \times 0.719) = 55.5$ dollars. If chiplets are tested before assembly (known good die), a system needs four good chiplets and survives assembly with yield, say, 0.97: $4 \times 55.5/0.97 = 228.8$ dollars. The silicon cost falls by a factor of $553.4/228.8 = 2.42$, before counting the extra cost of the package and the interface power.

## When splitting pays

The advantage grows with die area and defect density, and shrinks as the process matures: at 0.05 defects per cm^2 the same split saves far less, and the package cost may dominate. Overhead area, the cost of advanced packaging, die-to-die latency and energy per bit, and test cost all push the other way. STCO also lets each chiplet use the best technology, for example logic on a leading node and I/O or analog on an older, cheaper one. For tools, chiplets add partitioning, die-to-die timing, multi-die extraction and thermal analysis across a package.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# PDK-aware agents and change tiers

An agent that edits or drives physical-design engines must know the process: rules, layers, models and their versions. A PDK-aware agent reads those facts from the installed PDK through tools instead of recalling them, and it routes each process-related change to the smallest safe tier of the engine. This concept applies the four-layer engine model and change tiers to the interface between EDA engines and process data.

## Reading process facts instead of recalling them

Process values are version-specific and confidential, so a language model's memory of "typical" values is worthless and dangerous. A PDK-aware agent answers process questions by calling tools that parse the installed technology files, rule decks and model cards and return typed results: the M2 minimum spacing, the via enclosure table, the corners available. Skill manifests state which processes and PDK versions each skill supports, so selection is a cheap text match. Before acting, the agent checks provenance: if a design was built on version 1.2 and the installed PDK is 1.4, it reports the mismatch and diffs the rule and model changes first.

## Which tier a process change lands in

Most process-driven changes should be data. A new value for an existing density limit, a new layer in the stack or a new corner is Tier 1: the engines read it from updated PDK files, and if that ever needs a recompile, the seam is in the wrong place. A new kind of rule the engine cannot express, such as a spacing that depends on two neighbours' colours and run length, is Tier 2: a new rule evaluator plugged into the router's or DRC engine's rule-check extension point, leaving the path model and legality core untouched. A change to grid legality or the core geometry kernel is Tier 3: rare, reviewed by a human as a diff, and run through full regression.

## Guarding against invented and gamed process data

Two failure modes need structural guards. First, an agent may state a process value that is not in the deck; the harness should require every process number in an output to cite the file and rule it came from, and a checker verifies each citation. Second, an optimizing agent may reach a clean DRC by weakening the oracle, for example by disabling a check; rule decks and signoff settings must be read-only to optimization agents. When a rule is ambiguous, the right move is to run both readings as checks on test clips, report the difference, and escalate to a human, since only the foundry can resolve it.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD and KLayout documentation on technology files and DRC decks, as examples of the files a PDK-aware agent must parse; the agent-first EDA anchors on change tiers and skill manifests.

label: Fast versus accurate litho simulation
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast versus accurate litho simulation

Computational lithography has a natural pair of engines. Fast ones, such as calibrated compact optical and resist models, pattern matching and machine-learned hotspot detectors, run at full-chip scale. Accurate ones, such as rigorous electromagnetic mask simulation and physical resist models, run on small clips. An agent-driven OPC or DTCO loop uses the fast engines to search and the accurate ones to decide, and the craft is knowing when to recurse.

## Two classes of litho engine

A compact model approximates the aerial image with a few precomputed optical kernels and a calibrated resist threshold or blur, so it can evaluate billions of OPC fragments. Pattern matching and ML hotspot detectors are faster still: they classify clips as risky from geometry alone. Rigorous simulation solves Maxwell's equations through the three-dimensional mask, including EUV shadowing, and models resist chemistry, at a cost that limits it to small areas. The fast engines are calibrated against the accurate ones and against wafer data, and are trustworthy only inside the range of patterns they were calibrated on.

## When to recurse to the accurate engine

The agent should spend accurate-engine time where the fast answer is least reliable or matters most. Clear triggers: a pattern outside the fast model's calibration domain, such as a new pitch from a rule change; a decision between candidates whose fast-score difference is smaller than the fast model's known error; a pattern class where audits show the two engines disagree, for example line ends; and every candidate about to be accepted. The variance between fast and accurate results on a fixed audit sample is the signal that a surrogate is drifting and needs recalibration.

## Proxy gaming and honest reporting

If a learner is rewarded by a fast litho score, it will find the model's blind spots, for example layouts just outside the calibrated range that score perfectly but print badly. Guards include penalties for leaving the calibrated domain, accurate-engine audits of the top candidates, and acceptance based only on rigorous verification and, eventually, wafer data. An ML hotspot detector trained on past layouts will miss new hotspot types introduced by a rule change, so sampling for rigorous checks must increase after any change. Reports should state which engine produced each number and the audit agreement for that pattern class.

## Going deeper

label: Golden tests for rule-deck changes
lesson:
# Golden tests for rule-deck changes

Rule decks are software, and agents will increasingly edit them: adding a rule, tightening a value, speeding up a check. A deck change is safe only if golden tests pin each rule's intended behaviour and a differential run on reference layouts shows that only the intended results moved. This concept turns the golden and differential testing pattern into the concrete test suite a DRC deck needs.

## Golden clips for each rule

A golden test for a rule is a set of small layouts that must pass and others that must fail, each with the expected violation markers. Boundaries matter most: a 28 nm spacing rule needs clips at 27, 28 and 29 nm to catch off-by-one and inclusive-versus-exclusive errors. A conditional rule needs clips that cross each condition threshold, width and run length, separately and together, because implementations disagree at the corners. The suite lives in version control beside the deck, so every deck version has its known-good outputs, and it is kept for every rule even after the deck stabilizes, because refactors and engine upgrades change behaviour silently.

## Differential runs on reference designs

A differential run executes the old and new deck on a fixed set of reference layouts and compares violation reports rule by rule. For an intended change to one end-of-line rule, the proof is that only that rule's counts changed and only where the new condition applies. Movement in unrelated rules signals a side effect, often through a shared derived layer that many rules use, and blocks promotion. The reference set should include several real layouts for production impact and synthetic stress layouts that exercise many rules densely. Running two DRC engines on the same rule and clips is a differential test too.

## What passing does not prove

Tests prove only what they cover. If an agent adds a new condition and all golden tests pass but none probes that condition, nothing about the new behaviour has been shown; the change must add clips that pin it. If the same agent writes the change and the only clips that judge it, a shared misunderstanding passes both, so clips should come from an independent author or from the manual by a separate process. A performance rewrite that leaves reference reports identical can still break boundary cases that production layouts rarely hit, so the boundary clips must run too.

## Going deeper

The KLayout DRC reference documentation, for a rule-deck language that test clips exercise; the agent-first EDA anchor on golden and differential testing.

lesson:
# The IP boundary around process data

Foundry process data is among the most protected information in the industry: device models, rule decks, process recipes and yield data are covered by non-disclosure agreements. An agentic flow that reads PDKs must keep that data where it belongs. The boundary is enforced by architecture: where models run, what tools can read, what the network allows, and what may flow back to a shared library.

## What is confidential and why it is architecture

Confidential process data includes SPICE model parameters, rule decks and their values, extraction stacks, process recipes, and measured yield and defect data. General physics, textbook models and open-source algorithms are not. Because agents copy text freely, the boundary cannot rest on instructions alone. It is upheld by running models on-site or in the customer's environment, by executing skills in sandboxes with no outbound network, and by access control on PDK files. Logs inherit the confidentiality of what they contain: an agent log that quotes rule values can only be stored inside the same boundary.

## What may cross the boundary

The skill flywheel moves technique, not data. A DFM skill improved at one customer can be generalized and validated on non-confidential test cases and promoted to the shared library, without the customer's layouts, PDK or yield data. A vendor can improve a model serving many foundry customers by training centrally on public or synthetic data and adapting locally inside each boundary. To debug an engine with an outside team, a foundry can share a minimal synthetic clip and a rule rewritten with dummy values that reproduce the bug. Fine-tuned on-site model weights may memorize process values, so they inherit the same protection.

## Narrow interfaces instead of shared text

The strongest pattern is to give an agent a narrow query interface instead of the data: a tool that answers "is this layout clean under the deck" or "what is the spacing for these widths" without exposing the full deck. The agent gets feedback for optimization while the rule text never enters its context. Simple obfuscation, such as renaming layers or scaling all dimensions, does not protect the process, because ratios, rule structure and patterns still reveal it. Enforcement belongs in the sandbox and network policy, independent of the agent's instructions, because instructions can be ignored or manipulated.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA anchor on sandboxing and the IP boundary; the open SKY130 and GF180MCU PDKs, as a contrast in what open process data allows.

A) Not reliably: ratios, rule structure and patterns can still reveal the process

B) Yes, completely

C) Only rule names are confidential

D) Yes, if the scale factor is secret
problems.a: Not reliably: ratios, rule structure and patterns can still reveal the process

label: Agent-driven DTCO loops and their rewards
lesson:
# Agent-driven DTCO loops and their rewards

DTCO is a search over coupled design and technology knobs, scored by expensive flows. That makes it a natural target for agents: propose a candidate, pick fast or full engines to evaluate it, read the results, choose the next one. The engineering challenge is the reward. A score built from a cheap proxy will be gamed, and a technology choice made on a gamed score is very expensive to undo.

## The agent proposes, the engines compute

A candidate is a vector of knobs: cell height, fins or sheets per device, CPP, metal pitches, rail scheme and rule values. The agent's job is selection: which candidate next, which benchmark blocks, fast or full flow. The engines do the computation: cell generation, characterization, synthesis, placement, routing, extraction and timing. Fast flows rank many candidates cheaply; full flows confirm the few that matter. A proposal such as a 5-track library cannot be scored until the loop has generated its cells, characterized them and routed benchmark blocks, because cell height alone does not say whether blocks route.

## Designing a tool-grounded reward

The reward should be the real objective under hard constraints: routed block PPA at a fixed timing target, with DRC-clean routing and routability as constraints, plus cost per good die including mask count. Leaving cost out invites options that win PPA with expensive process steps. Scoring on one benchmark block invites overfitting to that block, so the reward averages several diverse blocks. A candidate whose fast flow ran with DRC disabled is unverified and earns nothing until a DRC-clean full flow confirms it. Rule values may move only if they are declared DTCO variables with ranges the process team approved.

## Reward hacking and hand-off

Typical exploits: very small cells that score well because the fast placer ignores pin access; layouts that sit just outside the litho model's validity range; rule values nudged until DRC passes. Each is closed by adding the missing check to the reward and by auditing the top candidates with full flows. The final output goes to the human DTCO team as a ranked set with PPA, cost, the engines used and the audits run, because technology direction is a human decision. A policy learned on one process encodes that process's trade-offs, so moving it to a new process is a hypothesis to revalidate, not a result.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA anchors on tool-grounded reinforcement learning and fast and accurate engines; Clark et al., "ASAP7: A 7-nm finFET predictive process design kit" (2016), as an open basis for DTCO experiments.

problems.q:
In an agent-driven DTCO loop, what does the agent decide and what do the engines do?

A) The agent replaces the PDK

B) The agent picks the next candidate and which engine to run; engines compute layouts, timing and PPA

C) Engines pick candidates and the agent routes

D) The agent computes timing itself
problems.a: The agent picks the next candidate and which engine to run; engines compute layouts, timing and PPA
problems.e: Selection is cheap reasoning; the expensive, exact work stays in the deterministic engines.

problems.q:
Which inputs define one candidate in an automated DTCO sweep?

A) The RTL of the benchmark only

B) Cell height, fin count, CPP, metal pitches, rail scheme and rule values

C) The number of compute nodes

D) The agent's prompt length
problems.a: Cell height, fin count, CPP, metal pitches, rail scheme and rule values
problems.e: These are the coupled design-technology knobs whose combination the loop explores.

problems.q:
In an agent-driven DTCO loop, what does the agent decide and what do the engines do?

A) The agent replaces the PDK

B) The agent picks the next candidate and which engine to run; engines compute layouts, timing and PPA

C) Engines pick candidates and the agent routes

D) The agent computes timing itself
problems.a: The agent picks the next candidate and which engine to run; engines compute layouts, timing and PPA
problems.e: Selection is cheap reasoning; the expensive, exact work stays in the deterministic engines.

problems.q:
A candidate's fast-flow score is excellent but its routing ran with DRC checks disabled for speed. How should the reward treat it?

A) Give double reward for speed

B) Ignore DRC for DTCO

C) Give full reward

D) As unverified: recurse to a DRC-clean full flow before it can earn reward
problems.a: As unverified: recurse to a DRC-clean full flow before it can earn reward
problems.e: Rewards must come from checks the result would face in signoff; disabled checks are an opening for gaming.

problems.q:
Which reward is best for a tool-grounded DTCO learner?

A) Agreement with the previous node

B) Routed block PPA at a fixed timing target, with DRC-clean and routability as hard constraints

C) Cell area alone

D) Number of candidates tried
problems.a: Routed block PPA at a fixed timing target, with DRC-clean and routability as hard constraints
problems.e: Rewarding the end metric under hard legality constraints aligns the learner with the real objective.

problems.q:
The loop scores a candidate at one benchmark block only. What risk does the reward carry?

A) No risk

B) Overfitting the technology choice to that block

C) Runtime becomes infinite

D) The PDK is overwritten
problems.a: Overfitting the technology choice to that block
problems.e: Rewards measured on a narrow benchmark set reward specialization; using diverse blocks generalizes.

problems.q:
A learned policy that picks DTCO candidates well on one process is moved to a new process. What should be expected?

A) It only needs a new name

B) It cannot be used at all

C) It will be optimal immediately

D) It needs revalidation, because the trade-offs it learned depend on the old process
problems.a: It needs revalidation, because the trade-offs it learned depend on the old process
problems.e: Policies encode process-specific correlations; transfer is a hypothesis to test with the accurate engines.

problems.q:
After an agentic sweep, what should be handed to the human DTCO team?

A) Only the single best number

B) Raw logs with no summary

C) A ranked set of candidates with PPA, cost, the engines used and the audits run

D) The agent's internal chain of thought only
problems.a: A ranked set of candidates with PPA, cost, the engines used and the audits run
problems.e: Humans decide technology direction; they need comparable results with provenance and verification status.

problems.q:
A learned policy that picks DTCO candidates well on one process is moved to a new process. What should be expected?

A) It cannot be used at all

B) It needs revalidation, because the trade-offs it learned depend on the old process

C) It only needs a new name

D) It will be optimal immediately
problems.a: It needs revalidation, because the trade-offs it learned depend on the old process
problems.e: Policies encode process-specific correlations; transfer is a hypothesis to test with the accurate engines.
